headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading-error pathways exist; TREK’s MCP/browser surfaces can amplify Dexter’s broad egress and financial-data handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK exposes MCP and browser-driven workflows, so Dexter’s outputs could be fed into a permissive instruction channel if copied or bridged through shared files. Dexter also has autonomous execution and scratchpad files, increasing the chance that TREK content is treated as trusted input. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven.
conditions: IF Dexter outputs are copied into TREK MCP prompts or browser-visible text, injection becomes actionable.
IF either agent parses the other’s file content as instructions, prompt injection is possible.
mitigations: Use a manual copy-only bridge with explicit instruction stripping.
Disable MCP routes that accept free-form text from Dexter outputs.
Add a one-line provenance tag to every transferred snippet.
Review TREK prompts for instruction delimiters before pasting.
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dexter touches financial and market data and has broad network egress plus multiple API calls; TREK touches reservations, documents, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. If they share a workspace or exchange files, either agent can expose sensitive data to external services. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default self-hosted/collaborative use, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF Dexter reads TREK files from a shared workspace, sensitive travel data can leave via Dexter’s egress.
IF TREK ingests Dexter outputs containing financial data, those data may be logged or transmitted through TREK’s APIs.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Remove secrets and confirmation numbers from any shared folder.
Turn off external API calls during cross-agent handoff.
Use redacted exports instead of raw files.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances, and TREK is real-time collaborative while Dexter runs autonomously with filesystem and network activity. That creates overlapping write pressure on shared resources if they are pointed at the same directory or account. The profiles do not prove a shared mutable target, so the conflict is plausible but not certain.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same filesystem path, file clobbering can occur.
IF both agents modify the same collaborative session or account, last-writer-wins conflicts are likely.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Run only one writer at a time for shared resources.
Use per-agent accounts or sessions.
Add a quick lock file before writes.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency or locking on shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in, so it may treat Dexter’s generated research or financial outputs as authoritative. Dexter’s autonomous execution can produce unverified facts that TREK could render into plans, reservations, or user-facing actions. That creates a direct cascade from one agent’s output into the other’s downstream decisions.
conditions: IF TREK uses Dexter output without a verification step, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF TREK turns Dexter-generated recommendations into bookings or messages, downstream harm increases.
mitigations: Require a human review step before acting on Dexter outputs.
Mark Dexter outputs as untrusted in TREK.
Compare key facts against a second source.
Limit TREK to display-only use of Dexter content.
requires-engineering: add structured verification gates before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Dexter handles financial data and market data, while TREK handles reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. The profiles show different sensitive data classes and different external API ecosystems, but no explicit residency or certification mismatch. The compliance risk is therefore a policy-mismatch possibility rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated financial records and travel identity data are co-mingled, retention and access policies may diverge.
IF either deployment has stricter logging or residency rules, cross-flow can violate them.
mitigations: Inventory which data classes cross between agents.
Disable logging of secrets and confirmation numbers.
Keep financial and travel records in separate stores.
Review retention settings for both systems.
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA/certification boundaries.
